video_title: Bitcoin Is the Hedge Against a U.S. Default Nobody Sees Coming
gist: VanEck CEO Jan van Eck lays out his three 10-year macro themes (India becoming Europe-sized, AI with now-projectable token demand, and US government spending as the biggest portfolio risk), predicting the US will fail to honor obligations such as Social Security payments within a decade and urging real assets, gold and Bitcoin as hedges. He also discusses VanEck's internal AI adoption (~$2M/yr spend, MCP data feeds to RIAs), the end of new single-asset crypto ETFs in favor of active management, 24/7 tokenized markets, and a shift of ETF flows toward direct individual investors.

themes.theme: US fiscal default risk and hard-asset hedges

insights.claim: Jan van Eck argues the next major US financial crisis will originate in Washington's fiscal position rather than in the banking system, unlike all previous US crises, and that no one can bail the US out.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Reframes systemic risk away from bank credit toward sovereign/fiscal risk, favoring assets outside the dollar-debt system.
insights.quote: for the entirety of US history, there's been financial crises that have come from the banking system or other industries, um, like agriculture and then rolled up through the banking system. This is going to be started in DC

insights.claim: Van Eck predicts the United States will fail to honor some of its obligations (which some would call a default) within the next 10 years, a view he says 99% of people he asks reject.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A contrarian, time-bound default call from a $235B asset manager CEO; supports long-duration hedges against sovereign credit erosion.
insights.quote: when is the United States not going to honor its obligations? Some people call that a default. And then I say it's going to happen in the next 10 years. And literally 99% of the people say no.

insights.claim: Van Eck points to 2032 as the year Social Security payments will be cut, and argues that covering the gap would require money-printing that causes massive inflation, meaning the US will inflate its way out of its debt.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete 2032 catalyst where the default-vs-inflation trade-off becomes explicit; bullish real assets, bearish long nominal bonds.
insights.quote: we're going to inflate our way out of our debt. It's it's there's no easy answer and it's not going to be pretty.

insights.claim: Van Eck says China's holdings of US Treasuries are down by half from their peak, and Chinese private investors (not just the central bank) are buying almost half of all gold production this year.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Foreign retreat from Treasuries plus private Chinese gold demand is a structural bid for gold and a headwind for US debt demand.
insights.quote: China's holding of treasuries is down by half from its peak and they are buying almost half of all gold production this year.

insights.claim: Van Eck recommends every portfolio hold real assets, gold and Bitcoin as insurance against government-spending risk, while admitting he does not know if or when the hedge pays off, which could be in 3 months or 30 years.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Frames gold and Bitcoin as structural allocations rather than timing trades; he is a long-term bull expecting significantly higher prices in 10 years.
insights.quote: you have to have real assets, gold, and Bitcoin in your portfolio. You don't know if it'll pay off.

insights.claim: Van Eck, whose father launched the first US gold fund in 1968, stresses he is not a gold bug, noting gold fell most of his career and bottomed at $250 an ounce around when the Bank of England sold, which makes his current structural gold call notable.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A self-described non-gold-bug turning structurally bullish on gold strengthens the signal; also a reminder that official-sector selling marked the bottom.
insights.quote: I am not a gold bug. It's hard to believe, but I do think this is just a structural risk.

insights.claim: Van Eck rejects the idea that AI's deflationary effect will rescue US fiscal finances, arguing government transfers for retirement and healthcare cannot shrink and new technologies like GLP-1s add demand for healthcare spending.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the popular 'AI productivity solves the deficit' narrative, keeping the inflation-hedge thesis intact.

insights.claim: Van Eck argues all technology is deflationary, citing the PC, the internet and Amazon, yet the 1970s still had runaway inflation despite great technology, so AI deflation does not preclude fiscal-driven inflation.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that monetary/fiscal inflation can overwhelm tech deflation; don't underwrite disinflation on AI alone.
insights.quote: all technology is deflationary. There were there was great technology in the 70s, but we had runaway inflation.

insights.claim: Van Eck believes the recent rise in US interest rates was driven by stronger nominal GDP growth rather than credit concerns or oil, noting the 10-year Treasury actually rallied at the start of the conflict with Iran.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: If yields reflect growth rather than credit stress, the fiscal crisis has not yet started pricing in, though higher rates still pressure portfolios.
insights.quote: the rise in rates recently was not credit driven.

insights.claim: Van Eck says voters punish politicians for inflation, which he believes partly got Trump elected, implying inflation is a politically constrained but likely path for handling US debt.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Political backlash to inflation is a friction on debasement, raising odds of messy outcomes such as benefit cuts.

insights.claim: VanEck's investment framework ignores day-to-day prediction and instead hunts for 10-year trends driven by four forces: big changes in government spending, monetary policy, regulation and technology, because asset allocation is the most important portfolio decision.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A simple screen for secular themes; his current output is AI, India, and government spending as the biggest risk.

insights.claim: Van Eck has very high conviction that India's economy will be the size of Europe's within 10 years, treating India's deregulation as comparable to China's pivot to price-based capitalism, the biggest deregulatory move of his career.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Supports long-horizon overweight to Indian equities on the view that the reform phase is done and now just 'playing out'.
insights.quote: I have very high conviction that India is going to be the size of of Europe in 10 years

insights.claim: Van Eck attributes India's growth to Modi's digitization of the economy (phones costing a couple of dollars a month and digital government ID) which let brokerages he met open a million accounts a month online during COVID.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Frictionless digital onboarding drives mass retail financialization, a tailwind for Indian brokers, fintech and domestic equity flows.
insights.quote: I met with brokerage firms that were opening a million accounts a month

insights.claim: Van Eck says India's sequential reforms of taxation, labor laws with employee-count thresholds, and bankruptcy laws removed distortions that had kept companies artificially at 9 or 999 employees.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Removing size thresholds lets Indian firms scale, supporting corporate earnings growth over the decade.
insights.quote: all companies, Anthony, were either nine, you know, nine people or 999, right?

themes.theme: AI token demand and enterprise adoption

insights.claim: Van Eck argues the AI trade is moving from a simple demand-exceeds-supply story to one where token demand can be projected like hamburger or Netflix subscription sales, which he expects to drive the trade going forward.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Forecastable token demand lets investors model AI infrastructure revenue more like a conventional business, sharpening winners vs. losers.
insights.quote: we have enough visibility that we can start projecting token demand.

insights.claim: VanEck's internal data shows a user's AI token usage rises about 8x in the first year of adoption and then grows about 25% annually, and extrapolating this to the industry matched other macro estimates of total token demand.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A bottom-up adoption curve (8x then 25%/yr) usable for modeling compute and inference demand growth.
insights.quote: in the first year, your token usage goes up eight times and then it grows about 25% after that annualized.

insights.claim: Van Eck notes that in Q4 of last year CoreWeave and Oracle fell 50%, illustrating that public markets punish AI names mercilessly on financing problems or tech changes even while overall demand is huge.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Expect violent drawdowns within the AI complex, especially for financing-dependent infrastructure names, despite secular demand.
insights.quote: the public markets are are merciless right when they smell uh financing problems or tech changes

insights.claim: Van Eck says corporate America's AI bottleneck is organizing data, citing PNC Bank spending $2 billion a year for 10 years to clean data, and links this to Accenture's stock bouncing after a massive correction.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Data clean-up and integration spend is a durable AI beneficiary; IT services firms like Accenture may be oversold as AI losers.
insights.quote: they spent $2 billion a year for 10 years just to clean up the data.

insights.claim: VanEck spends roughly $2 million annualized on AI and refuses to throttle employee usage despite CFO concern, arguing that forms or limits create friction and send the wrong signal on adoption.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Mid-sized asset managers are spending meaningfully and uncapped on AI seats/tokens, supporting enterprise AI revenue growth.
insights.quote: No, don't create friction for the adoption of this technology.

insights.claim: VanEck's IT department has been largely repurposed from writing code to connecting AI to internal databases, such as a connection to custodian State Street holdings data, which Van Eck says kills a huge part of the IT department's traditional work.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: AI connectors displace internal IT/reporting labor in financial firms, a margin tailwind for asset managers.
insights.quote: it that kill it just really kills a huge part of the IT department.

insights.claim: Van Eck, whose firm has 13 crypto ETFs in Europe, believes the era of launching more single-asset crypto ETFs is basically over and is pushing actively managed crypto funds because most advisers cannot pick between assets like Avalanche and Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Altcoin ETF launches may see diminishing flows; distribution shifts to index and active crypto products.
insights.quote: I think the days of sort of more crypto ETFs are basically over.

insights.claim: Van Eck thinks the two crypto categories most likely to survive are foundational layer-1 blockchains and exchanges, while being unsure whether Hyperliquid survives and noting BNB is not a perfect play on Binance.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A simple crypto selection filter: own L1s and exchange exposure, otherwise use an index or active fund.

insights.claim: Van Eck says firms like Franklin and Fidelity are rebuilding Wall Street's back end for 24/7 operation using blockchain, citing Franklin's money market fund offered to Uber users that is accurately priced over weekends.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Tokenization is advancing invisibly via incumbents, favoring large asset managers that own the plumbing.
insights.quote: the dream actually of most blockchain enthusiasts is you don't know that you're using it.

insights.claim: Van Eck sees upcoming sports ETFs as the most interesting development for the ETF industry because they essentially require 24/7 trading, since games happen at night and on weekends.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: New product categories could force ETF trading beyond exchange hours, pressuring incumbent market structure.

insights.claim: Van Eck says Hyperliquid has proven retail demand to trade hot assets over the weekend (e.g., pricing Anthropic or SpaceX, or gold in Q1), and the key fight to watch over the next year or two is incumbents like the CME suing the CFTC to protect their institutional franchise.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Regulatory outcome of the CME vs. CFTC fight determines whether 24/7 retail perps venues erode exchange incumbents.
insights.quote: the entrenched players like the CME are suing the CFTC. They're really fighting

themes.theme: Agents and the shifting ETF distribution model

insights.claim: Van Eck is skeptical of an 'agentic bank run' where AI agents shift deposits en masse to high-yield accounts, arguing banks provide services like fraud protection that people still want, and sees no equivalent risk for ETFs.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Downplays an emerging tail-risk narrative for bank deposit franchises.

insights.claim: Van Eck predicts people will give AI agents access to accounts with money, comparing it to auto-renew bill payments that already let companies' software pull from bank accounts.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Agent-initiated allocation and payments becomes a new distribution channel for funds and fintech.
insights.quote: I think that people are going to want to give their agents access to accounts with money in it.

insights.claim: VanEck's global web traffic is stagnant or falling, which Van Eck attributes to AI, and the firm is piloting an MCP connection giving an RIA client's agents direct access to its website data and documents, reportedly as BlackRock is also doing.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Fund distribution is shifting from web search and salespeople to agent data feeds, consistent with pressure on Google's ad-based search revenue.
insights.quote: our web track traffic around the world is is stagnant or falling

insights.claim: Van Eck predicts that within five years individual investors buying directly through low-cost broker-dealers will make up a quarter to a half of VanEck's business, up from a model dominated by financial advisers.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Direct-to-consumer ETF flows favor low-cost brokers and issuers with strong content and brand.
insights.quote: I'm going to say from a quarter to a half of our business.

insights.claim: VanEck manages about $235 billion with roughly 550 people, and about half its inflows over the last couple of years have come from Europe and Asia.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Non-US demand is a major driver for US ETF issuers' growth.
